posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring compliance pain post with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the auditability problem from a founder's perspective, add the 'explainability is the real unlock' insight without pitching
posts.draft_comment: The ban isn't really about ChatGPT — it's about the audit trail, or the lack of one. Numbers without a lineage are just guesses with confidence. The weird thing is most BI tools have the same problem, just dressed up in dashboards so it's less obvious. What would actually change the calculus for your team — full source tracing, or something else?

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO at 140-person firm hit the classic adoption wall — validate that trust is the real product, not the dashboard
posts.draft_comment: The dashboard was never really the deliverable. Trust in the numbers is. And trust gets built slowly — through someone quoting a figure in a meeting, being right, and others noticing. How long did it take before anyone on your team was willing to stake their reputation on something it produced?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post that validates dashboard overload — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add depth on why usage is the real metric, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is basically a graveyard of good intentions. The jump from 10% to 85% usage tells you more about what the dashboard was actually for than any of the metrics on it. The hardest conversation in BI isn't 'what should we measure' — it's 'who is actually going to open this thing on a Tuesday morning and change something because of it.'

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail is engaging on a post about BI chaos — validate the 'who owns the truth' pain with a sharper framing around semantic consistency, not tool choice
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports thing is so real — and the kicker is usually that everyone thinks their version is correct. The problem isn't that people got access to data, it's that the data was never given a shared meaning before the licences went out. Governance sounds boring until you're in a board meeting and the CFO's number doesn't match the CMO's number and everyone's staring at their laptops. Who owns the definition is a harder question than who owns the tool.

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO framing AI hallucinations as a security risk (not just accuracy) — validate the reframe, add a sharper distinction between hallucination types that makes the risk more concrete
posts.draft_comment: The reframe from accuracy problem to security problem is the right one, and I don't think the industry has caught up to it yet. There's a difference between an AI getting a number slightly wrong and an AI confidently fabricating a metric that never existed — the second one looks identical in a polished report. The scary part isn't that it happens. It's that most orgs have no audit trail to even know when it did.

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: CEO at 65-person firm naming the exact pain Milo was built to solve, with a COO prospect watching — validate hard with a specific observation, add the 'built for who' insight
posts.draft_comment: That £200k number is almost always the smaller problem. The real cost is 18 months of people just not trusting the numbers, going back to spreadsheets, and the whole thing quietly dying. Most BI tools assume someone technical is sitting between the data and the decision — and in a 50-person company, that person doesn't exist, or they're doing six other jobs. Who actually ends up owning it in your clients' businesses after the implementation team leaves?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director surfacing a classic data trust problem — validate that culture is the root cause, but add the nuance that tooling either hides or exposes the mess.
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, same dataset, three answers — that's not a filter problem, that's a trust collapse waiting to happen. The CFO doesn't care who applied which filter. They just stop believing the dashboard. Culture has to own the definitions, but someone still has to make those definitions impossible to accidentally break — whose job is that in your org?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing real enterprise AI adoption failure — validate the shadow AI insight and reframe the root cause as a data literacy problem, not a tool problem
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number is pretty telling, but the shadow AI piece is the real signal. When people sneak off to ChatGPT on their phones, they're not rejecting the approved tool — they're rejecting the friction of not knowing what they're supposed to be doing with data in the first place. No tool fixes that. What does your onboarding actually teach people to *ask*?
